title: HOLC Grades New York City
description: The Home Owners' Loan Corporation grades New York's neighborhoods A through D. Harlem and Bedford-Stuyvesant, already home to large Black communities, are graded D ("Hazardous"), as are Mott Haven, Melrose and Morrisania in the South Bronx — then largely Irish, German, Italian and Jewish neighborhoods that became majority Black and Puerto Rican in the 1950s. Historians find the maps recorded and codified racial judgments that the FHA and private lenders were already applying.

title: First BQE Section Opens
description: The Brooklyn-Queens Expressway's first section, at Meeker Avenue and the Kosciuszko Bridge, opens; the full road is finished in 1964. Its Hicks Street trench will separate Red Hook from the rest of Brooklyn. Nearby, the elevated Gowanus Parkway opens over Third Avenue in Sunset Park in 1941.

title: Cross-Bronx Expressway Construction Begins
description: Robert Moses routes the expressway through East Tremont. In 1953 his alignment is approved over an alternative along Crotona Park backed by Bronx Borough President James Lyons. About 4,000 families are displaced, roughly 1,500 of them in East Tremont, and 159 apartment buildings are demolished in East Tremont and Morris Heights.

title: Federal Highway Money Arrives
description: The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 pays 90% of Interstate costs. The Major Deegan is finished that year, and the Bruckner Expressway (from 1957) and the Long Island Expressway's Queens sections push highways deeper into the Bronx and Queens.

title: Jacobs and the Lower Manhattan Expressway
description: A committee led by Jane Jacobs wins a December 1962 Board of Estimate vote against the Lower Manhattan Expressway, which would have cut through what is now SoHo, Little Italy and Chinatown. The plan is revived, then dropped for good in 1969.

title: Civil Rights Act Passes
description: The Civil Rights Act outlaws discrimination in public accommodations and employment; the Fair Housing Act follows in 1968. By then highway routes and decades of lending patterns had already shaped where New Yorkers could live.

title: The Bronx Burns
description: Through the 1970s, fires and abandonment destroy large parts of the South Bronx, as landlords walk away from buildings and the city closes fire companies. Charlotte Street becomes a national symbol after President Carter's 1977 visit.

title: NYC Fiscal Crisis
description: New York City nearly defaults. Deep cuts to fire, sanitation, schools and hospitals hit already disinvested neighborhoods such as the South Bronx, Central Brooklyn and Harlem hard.

title: First Toxics Release Inventory Data
description: EPA publishes the first Toxics Release Inventory data (reporting year 1987). Turn on the TRI layer to see where registered facilities are today.

title: Crack Epidemic and Mass Incarceration
description: The crack epidemic and aggressive policing hit Brownsville, East New York and the South Bronx hard — neighborhoods where much of the land had been graded D in 1938.

title: September 11 Attacks
description: The destruction of the World Trade Center devastates Lower Manhattan. Nearby Chinatown faces years of economic hardship from street closures and lost business.

title: Greenpoint–Williamsburg Rezoning
description: The Bloomberg administration rezones the Greenpoint–Williamsburg waterfront from industrial to high-rise residential use, one of more than 100 rezonings that reshape neighborhoods and accelerate rising rents.

title: Hurricane Sandy
description: Sandy kills 44 New Yorkers and causes about $19 billion in damage and lost economic activity in the city. Public housing on the waterfront, including Red Hook Houses and Coney Island, goes without power for weeks.

title: Gentrification in Formerly Redlined Neighborhoods
description: Harlem, Bedford-Stuyvesant, Bushwick and Crown Heights — much of it graded C or D in 1938 — see fast-rising rents and the displacement of long-time residents.

title: COVID-19 in Queens
description: COVID-19 hits Corona, East Elmhurst and Jackson Heights among the hardest in the city. Their 1938 grades were mixed — Corona D, Jackson Heights B and C — a reminder that today's disparities follow more than the HOLC lines.

title: Hurricane Ida
description: The remnants of Ida kill 13 people in New York City, 11 of them in basement apartments in Queens and Brooklyn.

title: Inequality Persists
description: Median household income is about $168,780 on the Upper East Side and $27,360 in Mott Haven/Melrose (2024, in 2025 dollars), roughly 6 to 1. Life expectancy differs by about 11 years between community districts.
